quote: Einstein did not comprehend the Bayesian methods; he lived before the cognitive biases were discovered; he had no scientific grasp of his own thought processes.
content: Einstein wrote about his own thought processes with more care than most scientists have: in his reply to Hadamard’s questionnaire on mathematical invention (Hadamard, The Psychology of Invention in the Mathematical Field, 1945), describing his thinking as “combinatory play” with visual and muscular images prior to words; in the Autobiographical Notes (1949), which set out his epistemology of free concepts constrained by experience; in “Physics and Reality” (1936); and in a long correspondence with Born on probability and with Schlick and Reichenbach on the philosophy of science. He also corresponded on probability with people who understood it and helped invent the statistics of bosons. The sensei’s dismissal is fiction, but it is fiction offered as the lesson, and the lesson depends on a fact that is false. The clause “barring that matter of the cosmological constant” dings Einstein, in a story, for the constant that the previous essay conceded “later turned out to be real” and declined to criticize him for; the two essays are a page apart and disagree about whether to blame him for being right.

quote: So no multiple dimensions. If we start doing anything that looks like we should call it ‘string theory,’ we’d better stop.
content: The students rule out the largest research programme in the field by fiat and rule in the author’s preferred speculations (timeless physics from Barbour, finitism, locality of entanglement) on the strength of an inscription in Lojban, which is what Privileging the Hypothesis, in this same book, calls the fallacy of raising a hypothesis to attention without evidence. Each hunch the students offer corresponds to a real programme, loop quantum gravity and causal sets for discreteness and the elimination of infinities, Barbour’s shape dynamics for timelessness, and none has produced a theory in the decades since, which is a fact about the difficulty of the problem rather than about the speed of the workers. Brennan’s “obvious” question, why the energy that is the eigenvalue of the Hamiltonian should be the energy that curves spacetime, is a real and known issue, since energy in general relativity is not a local observable and the Hamiltonian constraint of canonical gravity vanishes, and it is treated in the literature the story calls Eld science. The class project is a fiction about speed; its physics is a reading list.
